title: Handling examination malpractice allegations fairly
description: A practical guide for Kenyan school principals on managing a suspected examination malpractice case fairly, thoroughly, and in line with proper process.
body:
When malpractice is suspected during or after an assessment, how the school handles the allegation matters as much as the underlying facts. A poorly managed process — rushed, unfair, or inconsistent — can produce an unjust outcome regardless of what actually happened, and can expose the school to legitimate challenge.

The first response — preserve evidence calmly

When malpractice is suspected during an assessment, the immediate priority is to preserve whatever evidence exists — the specific material or behaviour observed, documented at the time, not reconstructed from memory afterward — while managing the situation calmly to avoid disrupting other candidates. Confronting the student aggressively in front of peers, while understandable as an instinct, rarely helps and can itself create procedural problems.

Documentation at the time of the incident

A written record, completed as close to the moment of the incident as possible — what was observed, by whom, at what time, with what evidence — is far stronger than a recollection written days later. This documentation should be factual and specific, avoiding interpretive language that goes beyond what was actually observed.

Important distinction: Document what was observed (a student was seen looking at another candidate's paper repeatedly) separately from the interpretation (the student was copying). The factual observation is defensible; the interpretation is a conclusion that the subsequent process should determine, not assume in advance.

Giving the student a genuine opportunity to respond

A fair process includes the student's own account of events before any conclusion is reached. This is not a formality — students sometimes have an innocent explanation for behaviour that appeared suspicious, and a process that reaches a conclusion before hearing this account risks a genuine injustice.

Following the examination body's specific procedures

National examination bodies have specific, defined procedures for reporting and managing suspected malpractice, which schools are required to follow precisely rather than improvising an internal process. Familiarity with these procedures in advance — not learned for the first time during an actual incident — ensures the school responds correctly under pressure.

Supporting the student through the process

Regardless of the eventual finding, a student facing a malpractice allegation is under significant stress, and the school's guidance and counselling function has a role to play in supporting them through the process itself, separate from the question of the eventual outcome.

Communicating with parents appropriately

Parents should be informed promptly and given a clear, factual account of what is alleged and what process will follow, rather than being left to learn about a serious allegation involving their child through indirect or delayed channels.

Maintain clear, timestamped records for any disciplinary process.
